title: Why Dreams Feel So Real
desc: Why does a dream feel exactly like being awake, until the moment you open your eyes? A calm, sourced deep dive into the science of dreaming: the night REM sleep was discovered, the brain areas that light up and the ones that go quiet, why your body stays still, how the outside world leaks into your dreams, what we really dream about, the big theories of why we dream, lucid dreamers who answered questions from inside a dream, and why dreams vanish when you wake. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. It ends with a slow wind-down, so you can listen until you drift off.

plan: b01: hook (you wake up sure it really happened: your heart is racing over something that never was) + 'Tonight, we'll explore' list + the question of the night: why does a dream feel exactly like being awake? Open loop: the brain may be doing the same work in both (paid off b04)

b02: the discovery of REM sleep: Aserinsky & Kleitman 1953 in Science (rapid eye movements in sleeping subjects, Chicago); Dement & Kleitman 1957 (sleepers woken in REM usually reported vivid dreams, far fewer in other stages); the night's cycles of about 90 minutes

b03: dreams outside REM: David Foulkes 1962 (thought-like mentation in non-REM sleep); Mark Solms 2000 Behavioral and Brain Sciences (dreaming and REM can be separated); Siclari et al. 2017 Nature Neuroscience ('posterior hot zone' activity predicts dreaming in both REM and non-REM)

b04: pay off b01 loop: why the dream world looks real: in REM, visual and emotional areas are highly active (Maquet et al. 1996 Nature PET: amygdala active, parts of prefrontal cortex quiet); Horikawa, Tamaki, Miyawaki & Kamitani 2013 Science (decoding what people saw in sleep-onset dreams from fMRI); the brain builds the same kind of model whether eyes are open or closed

b05: why the weirdness doesn't strike you: reduced activity in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during REM (Maquet 1996; Braun et al. 1997 Brain), weaker self-reflection and reality testing; dream bizarreness (Hobson); memory for context is patchy, so a sudden scene change feels normal

b06: why your body doesn't act it out: REM atonia; Michel Jouvet's work in the 1960s showing cats with brainstem lesions moving during REM as if acting out dreams; REM sleep behaviour disorder described by Schenck et al. 1986; sleep paralysis when atonia lingers into waking (Sharpless & Barber 2011 Sleep Medicine Reviews review, about 8% of the general population at least once); calm, factual, no medical advice

b07: the world leaking into dreams: Dement & Wolpert 1958 (spraying water on sleepers' skin often showed up in dream reports); alarm clocks and sounds becoming part of the story; smells and dreams (Schredl et al. 2009, odours changed the emotional tone of dreams); why a real sound can feel like it started inside the dream

b08: what we actually dream about: Calvin Hall & Robert Van de Castle 1966 content-analysis system and its norms; G. William Domhoff's continuity hypothesis (dreams reflect waking concerns); negative emotions such as fear and worry are common in dream reports; ordinary settings more than fantastic ones

b09: why we dream, part one: Hobson & McCarley 1977 American Journal of Psychiatry activation-synthesis hypothesis (the forebrain makes a story out of brainstem signals); Antti Revonsuo 2000 Behavioral and Brain Sciences threat-simulation theory (dreams as rehearsal); what each explains and what critics say

b10: why we dream, part two: memory: Stickgold et al. 2000 Science (people who played Tetris saw falling blocks at sleep onset, even amnesic patients); Wamsley, Tucker, Payne, Benavides & Stickgold 2010 Current Biology (those who dreamed about a virtual maze task improved much more after a nap)

b11: dreams and feelings overnight: Walker & van der Helm 2009 Psychological Bulletin ('overnight therapy': REM sleep may soften the emotional edge of memories); Rosalind Cartwright's studies of dreams after divorce; evidence is mixed and still debated; gentle, no clinical advice

b12: knowing you are dreaming: lucid dreams; Stephen LaBerge et al. 1981 (pre-agreed eye-movement signals from inside a lucid dream, Stanford); Saunders et al. 2016 meta-analysis (about half of people report at least one lucid dream); Konkoly et al. 2021 Current Biology (two-way communication with lucid dreamers: they answered simple maths questions with eye movements)

b13: why dreams vanish when you wake: Eichenlaub et al. 2014 Neuropsychopharmacology (high dream recallers show more brief awakenings and different brain responses); why writing a dream down right away helps (dream diaries, Schredl's research on dream recall); the fading feeling is normal

b14: practical takeaways (dreams are your brain's world-model running offline, the strangeness is a feature of a quieter prefrontal cortex, a dream diary if you want to remember more), callback to the opening (that racing heart over something that never happened), then a slow guided wind-down toward sleep, then the @end segment teasing 'The Hidden Reason You Talk to Yourself'
